pos: n. (elder son of Merari and head of the Mahlite family of Levites, who carried the boards, bars, pillars and sockets of the tabernacle)
etymology: From Hebrew Machli, connected with chalah, to be weak or sick — a name of no evident bearing on the man. Exodus 6:19 spells it Mahali; Numbers and Chronicles give Mahli.
biblical_def: Mahli is the firstborn of Merari, the third son of Levi, and the head of one of the two Merarite houses: “the sons of Merari; Mahli, and Mushi. These are the families of the Levites according to the house of their fathers” (Num 3:20), and again, “Of Merari was the family of the Mahlites, and the family of the Mushites” (Num 3:33). Their charge in the wilderness was the heaviest and least visible part of the tabernacle: not the ark and not the vessels, but the frame — the boards, the bars, the pillars, the sockets and the pins, all the ironmongery of a portable sanctuary. Because their burden was timber and bronze rather than holy things carried on the shoulder, they were given wagons: “four wagons and eight oxen he gave unto the sons of Merari, according unto their service, under the hand of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest” (Num 7:8). The Mahlites appear again and again through the Chronicler's rolls, and once more at the very end of the Old Testament story: the man of understanding whom Ezra's messengers found at Casiphia, without whom the second return would have gone up with no Levites at all, was “of the sons of Mahli, the son of Levi, the son of Israel” (Ezr 8:18).

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that the unseen structural work of God's house is a divinely assigned ministry, not a lesser grade of one.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Mahli is the head of a Levitical family and nobody has contested him. What his house sets against the modern church is a doctrine of the unglamorous. Numbers assigns the Kohathites the ark, the table, the candlestick and the altars, borne on the shoulder and covered by the priests; the Gershonites take the curtains and hangings; and the Merarites — Mahli's house — take the frame. Boards, bars, pillars, sockets, pins and cords. Nobody looks at a socket. But the sanctuary does not stand without them, and God named the men who carried them and appointed wagons for the load.

The principle to recover is Paul's, argued at length precisely because congregations have always got it wrong: the parts of the body which seem to be more feeble are necessary, and God has tempered the body together, “giving more abundant honour to that part which lacked” (1Co 12:24). A church that honours only the visible gifts has adopted a doctrine of ministry the Pentateuch already refuted in its assignment of wagons. The man who keeps the building sound, the accounts straight and the doors open is doing the Merarite's work, and it was never the case that God valued the curtains above the sockets that held them up.

pos: n. (younger son of Merari and head of the Mushite family of Levites, whose descendants served in the temple courses under David)
etymology: From Hebrew Mushi, of uncertain derivation, perhaps connected with a root meaning to withdraw or depart. He is never named apart from Mahli his brother.
biblical_def: Mushi is the second son of Merari and the head of the Mushites, one of the two Merarite families of Levites (Exo 6:19; Num 3:20). Like his brother's house, his descendants carried the frame of the tabernacle through the wilderness. Where the record grows interesting is in the Chronicler, who traces the family into the settled worship of the temple. “The sons of Mushi; Mahli, and Eder, and Jeremoth, three” (1Ch 23:23) — and the son named Mahli after his uncle shows a family keeping its own memory. When David organized the Levites into courses for the house that Solomon would build, the Mushites were numbered in: “The sons also of Mushi; Mahli, and Eder, and Jerimoth. These were the sons of the Levites after the house of their fathers” (1Ch 24:30). And centuries after that, when Josiah repaired the temple, the overseers of the workmen included “Jahath and Obadiah, the Levites, of the sons of Merari”, and the record adds that the men did the work faithfully (2Ch 34:12). Wilderness, monarchy, reformation: the same house, doing the same kind of work, for the better part of a thousand years.

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is generational faithfulness — a house serving God in the same office across centuries, and a father's duty to hand on what he received.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Mushites are a Levitical family and no controversy attaches to them. What their record supplies is a picture the modern church badly needs: continuity. The same house appears carrying boards in the wilderness, standing in David's courses, and overseeing Josiah's repairs, and Chronicles is careful to say of that last generation that they did the work faithfully. Nothing in it is spectacular. It is a family that kept doing its assigned work while kingdoms rose and fell around it.

The principle to recover is the deliberate handing-on of the faith from one generation to the next, which Scripture treats as a command rather than a hope. “And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house” (Deu 6:7); “the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). A culture that treats each generation as free to reinvent its convictions produces exactly what Judges describes — a generation which knew not the LORD, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel (Jdg 2:10). The Mushites are the alternative, and their monument is a single line in Chronicles about doing the work faithfully.

pos: n. (second son of Kohath and head of the Izharites; the father of Korah, who led the rebellion against Moses)
etymology: From Hebrew Yitshar, fresh oil, from a root meaning to glisten — the word used for the anointing oil and the oil of the offerings. Numbers spells the name Izehar in one place.
biblical_def: Izhar is the second of Kohath's four sons: “the sons of Kohath; Amram, and Izhar, and Hebron, and Uzziel” (Exo 6:18). His elder brother Amram fathered Moses and Aaron; Izhar fathered Korah. Those two facts standing side by side explain the whole tragedy of Numbers 16. “And the sons of Izhar; Korah, and Nepheg, and Zichri” (Exo 6:21), and Korah, first cousin to Moses and Aaron, born into the most privileged Levitical house in Israel, wanted the priesthood as well: “Now Korah, the son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi… took men” (Num 16:1). The Kohathites already had the highest charge of any Levites, bearing the ark and the holy vessels themselves; Korah wanted the altar too. Moses put the question to him plainly — seemeth it but a small thing unto you, that the God of Israel hath separated you to bring you near to Himself, and seek ye the priesthood also? The Izharites survived their most famous son. They are numbered in David's courses (1Ch 23:18; 1Ch 24:22), and one of them, Shelomith, was set over the treasures of the dedicated things. The house whose head's name means fresh oil produced both the rebel and, afterwards, the sons of Korah who wrote psalms.

Of the sons of Izhar; Shelomith the chief.
corruption_summary: Korah's demand is admired as a protest against priestly monopoly, when Scripture presents it as discontent with a high calling already given — the same discontent that ruined Eden.
corruption_paragraphs: The Izharites were Kohathites, and the Kohathites carried the ark. No family in Israel outside the priesthood stood closer to the holy things. That is exactly what makes Moses' question to Korah so searching: “seemeth it but a small thing unto you, that the God of Israel hath separated you from the congregation of Israel, to bring you near to himself… and seek ye the priesthood also?” (Num 16:9-10). The sin is not ambition in the abstract; it is contempt for a real and enormous gift because a different one was withheld. That is the serpent's argument in Eden, made to people in a garden about the one tree they did not have, and it works the same way every time.

Modern readings often invert the passage into a fable about hierarchy and access. The dictionary reads it as Scripture reads it — and Scripture is emphatic that the priesthood is not seized but given: “no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron” (Heb 5:4), a sentence written about Christ. The gospel does grant every believer a priesthood, a real and glorious one — “ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood” (1Pe 2:5) — but by the gift of the one Mediator, not by the assertion of a right. And it is worth remembering how the story ends: the earth swallowed the men, but “the children of Korah died not” (Num 26:11), and their descendants wrote eleven psalms, one of which begins by longing for the courts of the LORD.

pos: n. (a recurring Levitical name: a son of Libni in the line of Gershom, an Izharite chief, and an overseer of the workmen in Josiah's repair of the temple)
etymology: From Hebrew Yachath, of uncertain derivation, possibly connected with a root meaning to snatch up or take hold. Four or five Levites of the name appear in Chronicles.
biblical_def: Jahath is a name that belongs entirely to the tribe of Levi. He stands in the Gershomite line in the Chronicler's genealogy of the singers — “Of Gershom; Libni his son, Jahath his son, Zimmah his son” (1Ch 6:20) — the ancestry that runs down to Asaph, who stood at David's right hand with cymbals. A Jahath heads a Shimeite house among the Levites David numbered (1Ch 23:10), and another is an Izharite: “Of the Izharites; Shelomoth: of the sons of Shelomoth; Jahath” (1Ch 24:22). The most memorable bearer appears at the end of the kingdom of Judah. When Josiah, having found the book of the law, set men to repair the house of the LORD, the record singles out the supervisors and the manner of the work in one sentence: “And the men did the work faithfully: and the overseers of them were Jahath and Obadiah, the Levites, of the sons of Merari; and Zechariah and Meshullam, of the sons of the Kohathites, to set it forward; and other of the Levites, all that could skill of instruments of musick” (2Ch 34:12). Levites overseeing carpenters, and musicians among them — the trades and the singers on the same site, with a Levite over both.

corruption_summary: Josiah's reformation is read as a pious tidying-up or as a late political invention, when Chronicles presents it as a nation recovering a lost book and rebuilding around it.
corruption_paragraphs: The critical commonplace is that the law-book found in Josiah's temple was written in Josiah's reign — a reforming party's programme presented as an ancient discovery. The dictionary rejects the reconstruction and holds Mosaic authorship. It is worth noticing what the theory requires: that the king, the high priest, the scribe, the prophetess and the assembled nation were either parties to a forgery or deceived by one, and that the deception produced a reformation whose chief effect was to tell Judah it was under a curse. Frauds are not usually designed to terrify their sponsors. What Chronicles describes is what the text says happened — a book neglected until it was lost in its own house, and a king who tore his clothes when he finally heard it read.

The second and more useful observation is about how reformation actually proceeds. It was not a mood; it was carpenters, masons, timber, hewn stone, and Levites keeping the accounts, of whom Chronicles says twice over that they dealt faithfully. Recovery of the word led directly to repair of the house and to the greatest passover since the days of Samuel. Genuine reform always takes that shape: the word first, then the ordinary obedience that follows it, and men counting money honestly because they have heard God speak. “to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word” (Isa 66:2) is Isaiah's standard, and Josiah's generation met it: “because thine heart was tender, and thou didst humble thyself before God” (2Ch 34:27).

pos: n. (a name borne by several Levites, singers and captains, including one of the fourteen sons of Heman and an overseer under Hezekiah)
etymology: From Hebrew Yerimoth, from rum, to be high — “elevations” or “heights”. Chronicles also spells it Jeremoth, and both forms stand in the KJV for the same name.
biblical_def: Jerimoth runs through the Chronicler's lists of the men who organized Israel's worship. He is a son of Mushi in the Merarite courses — “The sons also of Mushi; Mahli, and Eder, and Jerimoth. These were the sons of the Levites after the house of their fathers” (1Ch 24:30). He is one of the fourteen sons of Heman the king's seer, all of them appointed to the ministry of song: “the sons of Heman; Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel, and Jerimoth…” (1Ch 25:4), and the lot for the fifteenth course fell to him with twelve of his sons and brethren (1Ch 25:22). Under Hezekiah, when the temple was cleansed and the people brought in tithes and offerings in such heaps that store chambers had to be prepared, a Jerimoth is one of the ten men appointed to manage them: “overseers under the hand of Cononiah and Shimei his brother, at the commandment of Hezekiah the king” (2Ch 31:13). Singing, and then counting what the singing brought in. The Chronicler is interested in both, and never treats the second as beneath the first.

corruption_summary: The ordered, appointed, rota-governed worship of Chronicles is dismissed as dead formalism, and the singers' ministry reduced to entertainment; Scripture treats both the order and the song as commanded service.
corruption_paragraphs: Chronicles devotes chapters to who sang, when, with what instrument, and in what order, and the modern reader is inclined to hear only bureaucracy. That is a failure of imagination about what worship is. David appointed the singers by lot, so that the humblest course had the same title to its week as the greatest, and the whole arrangement was “according to the order of the king” — itself given, Chronicles says elsewhere, by the commandment of the LORD by His prophets (2Ch 29:25). Order in worship is not the enemy of life in worship; it is the form life takes when it is offered to a God who is not mocked. The regulative principle stands on exactly this ground: God says how He will be approached.

The second corruption is the modern reduction of church music to a means of producing feeling. The Chronicler will not have it. These men are said to prophesy with harps, psalteries and cymbals; their business was the word of God set to music and sung back to Him. Paul keeps the same standard: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16). Singing is teaching. A congregation is catechized by what it sings far more thoroughly than by what it hears preached, which is why the content of the songs is a matter of doctrine and not of taste.

pos: n. (a name borne by both men and women in Scripture: the Danite mother of the blasphemer, an Izharite chief, a keeper of the dedicated treasures, and a daughter of Zerubbabel)
etymology: From Hebrew Shelomith, from shalom, peace — “peaceful”. The irony of the first bearer's appearance in Leviticus is not lost on the reader; the name means peace and the episode is a stoning.
biblical_def: Shelomith is one of the few names in Scripture borne by both men and women. The first is a woman of Dan, named in a passage nobody forgets: her son, whose father was an Egyptian, strove with a man of Israel in the camp and “blasphemed the name of the LORD, and cursed. And they brought him unto Moses: (and his mother's name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan)” (Lev 24:11). The man was put in ward until the mind of the LORD should be shown, and the law given there governs the case for ever — and applies alike to the stranger and to the homeborn (Lev 24:16). The other bearers are Levites and royalty. “Of the sons of Izhar; Shelomith the chief” (1Ch 23:18) heads an Izharite house in David's courses. Another, of the line of Eliezer, held one of the great trusts of the kingdom: he “and his brethren were over all the treasures of the dedicated things, which David the king, and the chief fathers, the captains over thousands and hundreds, and the captains of the host, had dedicated” (1Ch 26:26) — the spoils of the wars, given to God. And a Shelomith is the sister of Meshullam and Hananiah, a daughter of Zerubbabel, named in the royal genealogy after the exile (1Ch 3:19).

corruption_summary: Blasphemy is now treated as a victimless offence against a fiction, and the third commandment as a rule about crude language; Scripture treats the name of God as the most serious thing a man can handle.
corruption_paragraphs: The blasphemy case in Leviticus 24 is the passage modern readers most want to explain away, and the explanations usually rest on the assumption that no real injury is done when a name is cursed. The Bible's premise is the opposite: God is, His name is Himself made known, and to curse it is the nearest a creature comes to striking at his Maker. The dictionary does not hold that the civil penalty of the Mosaic judicial law binds the modern state; those judicial laws expired with the nation to which they were given, their general equity only remaining. It does hold that the offence is exactly as grave as Leviticus says it is, and that the third commandment is not chiefly about coarse speech. “Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain” (Exo 20:7) — the commandment with a threat attached to it.

Two further things in the passage are worth naming because they cut against modern assumptions in both directions. First, the law is applied without partiality: “as well the stranger, as he that is born in the land”. The son of an Egyptian father received exactly the justice an Israelite would have received, neither harsher nor lighter, which is the biblical rule for courts — ye shall not respect persons in judgment. Second, the mother is named and her tribe given, and the record then leaves her alone. Scripture does not sentence Shelomith for her son's sin; the man who blasphemed bore his own iniquity, as Ezekiel would later insist at length: “The soul that sinneth, it shall die” (Eze 18:20).
roots_summary: Hebrew Shelomith (H8019), Shelomith, peaceful; shalom (H7965), peace; naqab (H5344), to pierce, to blaspheme by pronouncing; qalal (H7043), to curse, make light of; qodesh (H6944), dedicated, holy.

Hebrew naqab (H5344) — to pierce, to specify, to blaspheme; the verb of Lev 24:11.
Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to be light, to curse, to treat with contempt; joined with it there.

usage: “His mother's name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri” — a name preserved in the hardest chapter.
“As well the stranger, as he that is born in the land” — one law, no partiality.
“Over all the treasures of the dedicated things” — the spoils of war, given to God and kept by a Levite.

pos: n. (a Levite name of the temple service: a Korahite over the baked offerings, a singer with harp before the ark, and a man who stood beside Ezra at the reading of the law)
etymology: From Hebrew Mattithyah, “gift of the LORD”, from mattanah, gift, with the divine name. The same name in later Greek is Matthias, and in shortened form Matthew.
biblical_def: Mattithiah is a Levite name attached to three quite different services, and the range is the interest of it. First, the kitchens: “And Mattithiah, one of the Levites, who was the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, had the set office over the things that were made in the pans” (1Ch 9:31) — a standing appointment over the baked meat offerings, which somebody had to hold and which the Chronicler thought worth recording by name. Second, the music: when David brought up the ark, Mattithiah is among the Levites appointed with psalteries and harps (1Ch 15:18; 1Ch 16:5), and a Mattithiah stands among the six sons of Jeduthun “who prophesied with a harp, to give thanks and to praise the LORD” (1Ch 25:3). Third, the word: at the great reading in Nehemiah, when Ezra stood on a pulpit of wood made for the purpose, Mattithiah is the first man named at his right hand (Neh 8:4). Pans, harp and pulpit — the whole compass of Levitical duty in one name, which means “gift of the LORD”. The office over the pans is as much a set office as the place beside the pulpit, and Scripture records both in the same tone.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Mattithiah; in sacred history it is the name of several Levites, singers and officers of the house of God.
webster_full: MATTITHIAH, n. The name signifies the gift of the LORD.
A Korahite Levite, the firstborn of Shallum, who had the set office over the things made in the pans.
A Levite appointed with psalteries and harps when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem.
One of the six sons of Jeduthun, who prophesied with a harp to give thanks and praise the LORD.
One who stood at the right hand of Ezra when the law was read upon the pulpit of wood.
scriptures: And Mattithiah, one of the Levites, who was the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, had the set office over the things that were made in the pans.

Asaph the chief, and next to him Zechariah, Jeiel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Mattithiah, and Eliab, and Benaiah, and Obededom: and Jeiel with psalteries and with harps; but Asaph made a sound with cymbals;

Of Jeduthun: the sons of Jeduthun; Gedaliah, and Zeri, and Jeshaiah, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah, six, under the hands of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with a harp, to give thanks and to praise the LORD.
Neh 8:4

And Ezra the scribe stood upon a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose; and beside him stood Mattithiah, and Shema, and Anaiah, and Urijah, and Hilkiah, and Maaseiah, on his right hand; and on his left hand, Pedaiah, and Mishael, and Malchiah, and Hashum, and Hashbadana, Zechariah, and Meshullam.
corruption_summary: Church work is graded into sacred and menial, with music and preaching at the top; Chronicles records the man over the baking pans in the same register as the man with the harp.
corruption_paragraphs: “The set office over the things that were made in the pans” is one of the most quietly subversive phrases in Chronicles. It is a permanent, named, inherited appointment — and it is baking. The same book that lists the singers by lot and the porters by gate lists the man over the pans, and never suggests he is doing something less than they. The New Testament makes the principle a command that reaches past church work entirely: “And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23) — written first to slaves. There is no secular half of a Christian's life for that work to fall into.

The second thing worth naming is Nehemiah 8:4, because it is the Bible's own picture of a preaching service and it differs from much that now passes for one. A wooden platform built for the purpose; a book opened above the people, who stand when it is opened; thirteen named men flanking the reader; the law read from morning until midday; Levites moving through the congregation giving the sense. Everything in the scene is organized around the text being understood. The furniture itself preaches: when the pulpit is built for the purpose and the book is opened on it, a congregation learns what the meeting is for before a word is said. “Give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13).

pos: n. (a name of the post-exilic period meaning “unto the LORD are mine eyes”; borne by a descendant of David, a temple porter, and men who put away strange wives)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Elyeho'enay, a whole sentence compressed into a name: 'elay, unto me, Yeho, the LORD, 'enay, mine eyes — “toward the LORD are mine eyes”. Ezra 8:4 gives the fuller spelling Elihoenai.
biblical_def: Elioenai is a name that is a confession, and its bearers cluster in the exile and the return — a period when a man had reason to make his son's name a statement of where he was looking. The Chronicler places one in the royal genealogy: “the sons of Neariah; Elioenai, and Hezekiah, and Azrikam, three” (1Ch 3:23), the house of David counted on generations after the crown was gone. Another is a temple porter, the seventh son of Meshelemiah in the courses David appointed: “Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, Elioenai the seventh” (1Ch 26:3). An Elihoenai the son of Zerahiah leads two hundred men up with Ezra (Ezr 8:4), and an Elioenai of the sons of Pashur is named among the priests who had taken strange wives and put them away (Ezr 10:22). The name is the psalmist's posture made permanent: “Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net” (Psa 25:15), and in the psalm of ascents, “so our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until that he have mercy upon us” (Psa 123:2). Parents in Babylon named their sons that, and their sons came home.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Elioenai; in sacred history it is the name of several men of the exile and return, and signifies toward the LORD are mine eyes.
webster_full: ELIOENAI, n. The name signifies unto the LORD are mine eyes; written also Elihoenai.
A son of Neariah, in the line of David after the captivity.
The seventh son of Meshelemiah, among the porters of the house of the LORD.
Elihoenai the son of Zerahiah went up with Ezra, and two hundred males with him.
Others of the name are found among the priests and people who put away the strange wives.
scriptures: And the sons of Neariah; Elioenai, and Hezekiah, and Azrikam, three.
Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, Elioenai the seventh.
Ezr 8:4
Of the sons of Pahathmoab; Elihoenai the son of Zerahiah, and with him two hundred males.
And of the sons of Pashur; Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethaneel, Jozabad, and Elasah.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that naming is confession — parents in exile put their theology into their children's names, and expected the children to live in it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Elioenai is a name in genealogies and nobody has troubled to dispute it. What it quietly witnesses to is a practice the modern world has almost entirely lost: naming as confession. In captivity, with the temple burnt and the throne empty, a father called his son “unto the LORD are mine eyes”, and the boy carried that sentence through his whole life, spoken by everyone who addressed him. Isaiah did the same deliberately with his own household: “Behold, I and the children whom the LORD hath given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel” (Isa 8:18).

The principle to recover is the parent's duty to set his household's face in a direction and to say so. Names are one small instrument of that; the larger ones are family worship, the Lord's day, and the plain daily teaching Deuteronomy commands. Joshua stated the matter in the form every father must eventually take up: “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15). A generation of children whose names, homes and habits say nothing at all about where their parents are looking should not surprise anyone by looking elsewhere themselves.

pos: n. (a name of the royal and Levitical registers: a son of Jeconiah and father of Zerubbabel in Chronicles, a repairer of the wall, and a treasurer counted faithful)
etymology: From Hebrew Pedayah, “the LORD hath ransomed”, from padah, to redeem by payment of a price, with the divine name. It is a redemption word, borne by men of the captivity.
biblical_def: Pedaiah appears at the most sensitive point in the royal genealogy. The Chronicler lists the sons of Jeconiah — “Malchiram also, and Pedaiah, and Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah” (1Ch 3:18) — and then says: “the sons of Pedaiah were, Zerubbabel, and Shimei” (1Ch 3:19), where Ezra, Haggai and Matthew all call Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel. The most natural reading is a levirate marriage: Shealtiel died childless, his brother Pedaiah raised up seed to him, and Zerubbabel is legally Shealtiel's and naturally Pedaiah's. Other bearers belong to the rebuilding. A Pedaiah the son of Parosh repairs a section of wall by the court of the prison (Neh 3:25); a Pedaiah stands at Ezra's left hand at the reading of the law (Neh 8:4); and a Levite named Pedaiah is one of the treasurers Nehemiah appointed, of whom he wrote the best sentence a treasurer can have written of him: “for they were counted faithful, and their office was to distribute unto their brethren” (Neh 13:13). A name meaning “the LORD hath ransomed”, worn by men whose whole generation had been ransomed out of Babylon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Pedaiah; in sacred history it is the name of a son of Jeconiah in the royal line, and of several men of the restoration.
webster_full: PEDAIAH, n. The name signifies the LORD hath ransomed or redeemed.
A son of Jeconiah, king of Judah, and in Chronicles the father of Zerubbabel.
Elsewhere Zerubbabel is called the son of Shealtiel, the brother of Pedaiah.
A Pedaiah, the son of Parosh, repaired a portion of the wall of Jerusalem.
A Levite of the name was made a treasurer over the treasuries, being counted faithful.
scriptures: Malchiram also, and Pedaiah, and Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah.
And the sons of Pedaiah were, Zerubbabel, and Shimei: and the sons of Zerubbabel; Meshullam, and Hananiah, and Shelomith their sister:
Neh 3:25
Palal the son of Uzai, over against the turning of the wall, and the tower which lieth out from the king's high house, that was by the court of the prison. After him Pedaiah the son of Parosh.

And I made treasurers over the treasuries, Shelemiah the priest, and Zadok the scribe, and of the Levites, Pedaiah: and next to them was Hanan the son of Zaccur, the son of Mattaniah: for they were counted faithful, and their office was to distribute unto their brethren.
corruption_summary: The Pedaiah-Shealtiel difference over Zerubbabel's paternity is presented as a flat contradiction; the levirate law that Scripture itself supplies accounts for it without strain.
corruption_paragraphs: Chronicles calls Zerubbabel the son of Pedaiah; Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai and Matthew call him the son of Shealtiel. The sceptical handling files this as an error and moves on. But the Old Testament contains a law that produces exactly this pattern: when a man dies childless his brother raises up seed to him, and “the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name be not put out of Israel” (Deu 25:6). Under that law a man has two fathers — one who begat him and one whose name he carries — and a careful register may record either. Chronicles is the genealogical book and gives the natural descent; the narrative and prophetic books give the legal line, which is the line that matters for the throne. The difficulty is not a seam in the text; it is the text using its own law.

The second thing to draw out is the name, because the generation that used it was making a claim. The LORD hath ransomed. These were men born in exile, in a land whose gods had apparently won, whose temple was ash and whose king was a prisoner eating at another man's table. To name a son “the LORD hath ransomed” in that setting is faith speaking in the past tense about a deliverance not yet seen. It is Jeremiah's promise taken at face value, and it was answered: “For the LORD hath redeemed Jacob, and ransomed him from the hand of him that was stronger than he” (Jer 31:11).

pos: n. (a recurring name in the registers; chiefly the grandfather of Elkanah and so an ancestor of Samuel the prophet)
etymology: From Hebrew Yerocham, “he is pitied” or “he findeth mercy”, from racham, to have compassion. It is a passive form: the man does not show mercy, he receives it.
biblical_def: Jeroham is a name the registers keep bringing back, and its most consequential bearer stands three generations above one of the great men of the Old Testament. The opening verse of 1 Samuel gives the pedigree: “there was a certain man of Ramathaimzophim, of mount Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephrathite” (1Sa 1:1), and the Chronicler confirms the Levitical descent, “Eliab his son, Jeroham his son, Elkanah his son” (1Ch 6:27). Elkanah was Hannah's husband; the son she wept for at Shiloh was Samuel. Nothing whatever is recorded of Jeroham himself. Other men of the name appear among the heads of houses in Jerusalem after the return (1Ch 9:12), among the archers who came to David at Ziklag (1Ch 12:7), and as father of one of the five captains Jehoiada took into covenant with him when he brought the boy Joash out of hiding and crowned him in the temple: “Azariah the son of Jeroham” (2Ch 23:1). A name meaning “he findeth mercy”, appearing in the ancestry of the prophet who anointed the first two kings of Israel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Jeroham; in sacred history it is the name of several men, chiefly the grandfather of Elkanah and ancestor of Samuel.
webster_full: JEROHAM, n. The name signifies he is pitied, or findeth mercy.
The father of Elkanah, and grandfather of Samuel the prophet.
The Chronicler places him in the Levitical line of Kohath.
A Benjamite of the name is reckoned among the heads of the fathers dwelling at Jerusalem.
Azariah the son of Jeroham was one of the captains taken into covenant by Jehoiada the priest.
scriptures: Now there was a certain man of Ramathaimzophim, of mount Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephrathite:
Eliab his son, Jeroham his son, Elkanah his son.
And Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchijah, and Maasiai the son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer;

And in the seventh year Jehoiada strengthened himself, and took the captains of hundreds, Azariah the son of Jeroham, and Ishmael the son of Jehohanan, and Azariah the son of Obed, and Maaseiah the son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat the son of Zichri, into covenant with him.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that God ordinarily prepares great deliverances through unremarkable households nobody was watching.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Jeroham is a name in a pedigree. What the pedigree does is worth pausing over: it opens the book of Samuel, which is to say it opens the history of Israel's monarchy, and it opens with a hill-country household of no importance. Four generations are named and not one of them is famous. Then a barren woman prays at Shiloh, is taken for a drunkard by a failing priest, and bears the man who will anoint Saul and David. The New Testament opens the same way, with a genealogy and then a village carpenter's betrothed.

The principle to recover is that God's public works are prepared in private and in obscurity. “God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1Co 1:27), and the pattern holds so consistently that it must be deliberate. Samuel came out of a quarrelling polygamous household in the hills; David from the sheepfold; the apostles from fishing boats. Christians are perennially tempted to look for the next work of God among the visible and the credentialed. The registers suggest looking instead at the sort of home Jeroham kept: unremarkable, unrecorded, and three generations upstream of a prophet.
